title: 75. Numeracy & Number Systems: Translating Number Inequalities into Intervals
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Translating a Linear Inequality into Interval Notation
questions.learningObjective: Translate a non-strict lower-bound inequality into interval notation.
questions.question: Which interval represents \(x \ge -2\)?
questions.explanation: The inequality \(x \ge -2\) includes \(-2\) and all numbers greater than \(-2\). Therefore, the interval is \([-2,\infty)\). The choice "\((-\infty,-2]\)" represents \(x \le -2\), which is the opposite direction.
questions.hint: Decide whether the solutions lie to the right or to the left of \(-2\) on the number line, then choose the bracket for the endpoint.

questions.concept: Translating a Strict Inequality into Interval Notation
questions.learningObjective: Translate a strict upper-bound inequality into interval notation.
questions.question: Which interval represents \(x < 3\)?
questions.explanation: The inequality \(x < 3\) includes all numbers less than \(3\) but excludes \(3\). Therefore, the interval is \((-\infty,3)\). The choice "\((-\infty,3]\)" incorrectly includes \(3\).
questions.hint: A strict inequality uses a parenthesis at the finite endpoint.

questions.concept: Translating a Double Inequality into Interval Notation
questions.learningObjective: Translate a two-sided inequality with an included upper endpoint into interval notation.
questions.question: Which interval represents \(-1 < x \le 4\)?
questions.explanation: The inequality \(-1 < x \le 4\) excludes \(-1\) because of the strict inequality \({<}\), and includes \(4\) because of the inequality \({\le}\). Therefore, the interval is \((-1,4]\). The choice "\([-1,4]\)" incorrectly includes \(-1\).
questions.hint: Check each endpoint separately and match the inequality symbol to the bracket type.

questions.concept: Translating a Double Inequality into Interval Notation
questions.learningObjective: Translate a two-sided inequality with an included lower endpoint into interval notation.
questions.question: Which interval represents \(2 \le x < 7\)?
questions.explanation: The inequality \(2 \le x < 7\) includes \(2\) and excludes \(7\). Therefore, the interval is \([2,7)\). The choice "\((2,7]\)" reverses the endpoint inclusion.
questions.hint: Use a square bracket for \({\le}\) and a parenthesis for \({<}\).

questions.concept: Translating an Inequality with Infinity into Interval Notation
questions.learningObjective: Translate a non-strict upper-bound inequality into interval notation.
questions.question: Which interval represents \(x \le 5\)?
questions.explanation: The inequality \(x \le 5\) includes \(5\) and all numbers less than \(5\). Therefore, the interval is \((-\infty,5]\). The choice "\((-\infty,5)\)" incorrectly excludes \(5\).
questions.hint: Infinity always uses a parenthesis, but the finite endpoint may use a bracket.

questions.concept: Translating an Inequality with Infinity into Interval Notation
questions.learningObjective: Translate a strict lower-bound inequality into interval notation.
questions.question: Which interval represents \(x > -3\)?
questions.explanation: The inequality \(x > -3\) includes all numbers greater than \(-3\) but excludes \(-3\). Therefore, the interval is \((-3,\infty)\). The choice "\((-\infty,-3)\)" represents \(x < -3\).
questions.hint: Decide on which side of \(-3\) the solutions lie on the number line before writing the interval.

questions.concept: Translating a Closed Double Inequality into Interval Notation
questions.learningObjective: Translate an inclusive two-sided inequality into interval notation.
questions.question: Which interval represents \(-5 \le x \le 0\)?
questions.explanation: Both endpoints are included because both inequalities use \({\le}\). Therefore, the interval is \([-5,0]\). The choice "\((-5,0)\)" excludes both endpoints.
questions.hint: Use square brackets when the endpoints are included.

questions.concept: Translating a Half-Open Double Inequality into Interval Notation
questions.learningObjective: Translate a half-open two-sided inequality into interval notation.
questions.question: Which interval represents \(1 \le x < 6\)?
questions.explanation: The inequality \(1 \le x < 6\) includes \(1\) and excludes \(6\). Therefore, the interval is \([1,6)\). The choice "\((1,6]\)" incorrectly excludes \(1\) and includes \(6\).
questions.hint: Match each endpoint to its inequality symbol.

questions.concept: Translating an Open Double Inequality into Interval Notation
questions.learningObjective: Translate an open two-sided inequality into interval notation.
questions.question: Which interval represents \(-4 < x < 2\)?
questions.explanation: Both inequalities are strict, so both endpoints are excluded. Therefore, the interval is \((-4,2)\). The choice "\([-4,2]\)" incorrectly includes both endpoints.
questions.hint: Strict inequalities use parentheses at both finite endpoints.

questions.concept: Translating a Compound Inequality with "or" into Interval Notation
questions.learningObjective: Translate alternatives joined by or into a union of intervals.
questions.question: Which interval notation represents \(x < -1\) or \(x \ge 3\)?
questions.explanation: The condition \(x < -1\) gives \((-\infty,-1)\), and the condition \(x \ge 3\) gives \([3,\infty)\). Because the two conditions are connected by "or", their union is \((-\infty,-1) \cup [3,\infty)\). The choice "\((-\infty,-1] \cup (3,\infty)\)" incorrectly includes \(-1\) and excludes \(3\).
questions.hint: Translate each inequality separately, then combine the intervals with a union symbol.
